This is true when we look at motion as a kind of change that stands opposite to rest. But when something moves from one place to another, it passes through a series of temporary positions before coming to rest in one fixed place. That final place is the endpoint of the movement. — ط مده
Having distinguished good and generosity as terms used for goals, the author now explains what good and generosity mean more broadly. — س ره

Suppose an agent performs an action for a goal. If there were no goal, the action would not happen. So the act’s being brought about depends on the goal, just as the agent’s ability to act depends on it. Since the agent acts by its own nature, the goal must be present in some way within that nature, not wholly outside it. The agent has a general, undirected state and a particular state directed toward an action. The action, too, has two levels: the action itself and the fuller state it reaches. A thing can therefore be viewed as the basic fact that it exists and as the fuller state toward which it moves. This is how each created thing has a goal through its cause. What has no further goal and is itself the goal is not made for something else. — ط مده
Put another way, in every action the agent seeks itself. For agents that can change, an incomplete self seeks its more complete state, even if it only imagines that state. — س ره

The goal that exists in what receives an action, or in someone other than the agent, need not be the final goal. It may be the goal of one action and then serve another goal in a later action, until the chain returns to the agent. For example, a carpenter may make a bed so that a ruler can sit on it. That does not prevent the ruler’s sitting from having its own goal, or the carpenter from also seeking payment or some other benefit that serves his own good. — س ره
The author seems to mean that one kind of goal is both a goal and an endpoint in the strict sense. This specific use agrees with the wider, everyday meaning of the word. — س ره

Consider their familiar division: “A thing either requires existence through itself, and so is necessary, or it does not.” Yet the Necessary Being is pure, simple existence, standing by itself. His existence does not come from a maker or depend on a subject in which He exists, for He has neither matter nor an essence distinct from existence. So “requires” here means that He does not need another to give Him existence. Similarly, when they say that a substance “stands by itself,” they mean that it does not exist in another thing as an accident does.

A final cause is knowledge of the good result of an action. In this case, the ultimate goal is God Himself, so the knowledge in question is God’s knowledge of His own essence and, through it, of all that depends on Him. The philosophers describe this as general knowledge of effects; Mulla Sadra holds that God knows them all in a single, undivided act of knowledge. Since God’s essence is the source of the action, this knowledge gives rise to creation without deliberation.

This is natural, created worship: the obedience built into the way each thing is made. It is not the worship required by religious law. The commentator distinguishes commands addressed to people, which leave room for choice, from God’s creative command, through which things and matter take on their nature and powers.

The author specifies earthly, animal worship because human worship, considered at that level, is nothing like the worship of the heavenly spheres and their inhabitants. They neither sleep nor grow weary. They worship God without interruption or exhaustion. And what is ordinary human knowledge beside that of the angels who are protected from error, especially those nearest to God? As the verse says:
Where is the Beloved, and where are you, deceiver? What has the light of eternity to do with those still farther astray?
But among human beings there is a group superior even to the angels, let alone the heavenly spheres. Of them another verse says:
Neither the heavens nor the angels possess What lies in the deepest heart of Adam's child.
These are the finest of God's servants and the choicest beings in creation, especially those who follow Muhammad most completely. It is said of them:
The Holy Spirit, in the gardens of the highest sanctuary, Has tasted the earliest fruit from our gardens.
And of their leader it is said:
If Ahmad were to unfold that majestic wing, Gabriel would remain overwhelmed forever.
The words of Farīd al-Dīn ʿAṭṭār of Nishapur apply to this whole group:
My child, day and night these seven turning circles Carry out their work for your sake.
The worship of the spirits is for you; Paradise and Hell reflect grace and severity toward you.
The holy ones have all bowed before you; Part and whole are immersed in your existence.
Do not keep looking down on yourself in contempt; None greater than you is possible in this order.
Your outward being is a part; inwardly you contain the whole. Even in humility, do not think yourself incapable.
When the time comes for the whole to rise in rank, The ranks of creation rise through your existence.

The reason is that a human being who has reached full perfection stands under the Greatest Name, the name Allah. Angels stand under names that express God's freedom from imperfection, such as the All-Holy and the All-Pure. The heavenly spheres stand under such names as the Everlasting, the Exalter, and the Lord. The complete human being knows all the divine names: both those that express God's being beyond comparison and those that describe how His qualities appear in creation.

Consider the difference. The spirit of a heavenly sphere remains bound to its sphere. But the spirit of a person in this highest human group becomes free—not only from the natural body, but even from the body of the world of images and, beyond that, from both worlds of form. Such a person casts off the two sandals and leaves the two worlds behind. An angel close to God may be a spirit free of bodily limitation, yet still does not possess knowledge of all the divine names in both of these ways.

These complete human beings bring the rising chain of existence to its highest point. Their intellects have risen beyond the need to use the body and its organs. It is as though they have already taken their bodies off while still wearing them. They stand opposite the pure intellects that mark the beginning of the descending chain. If any veil remains, it will be lifted entirely. This is why ʿAlī said, as his earthly life ended, “By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have succeeded!”

Their worship is therefore nobler in quality than the constant worship of the heavens. A small amount of perfectly sincere action can outweigh an immense quantity of other actions. Their knowledge likewise surpasses the angels' knowledge, because the complete human being knows God through all His names. Perhaps, then, the author's statement concerns human beings simply as earthly human beings, not those who have reached this complete state. — S. R.
A thing can be the true goal only through its own independent perfection. Created beings do not exist independently; their existence depends on God. So God is their true goal.

More precisely, God is first through His self-subsisting existence and last as the goal toward which we turn. The commentator says that nearness to God means taking on divine qualities; Mulla Sadra calls this resembling the First Principle.

This explains why some goals that seem lower than the person can still be pursued. A poor writer seeks payment, which is a better state than being in need. Someone who is generous only in possibility seeks to become generous in action. In general, people seek a fuller state of themselves. The commentator adds that the intention itself is higher than the thing intended, because the intention gives rise to the action.

The lower goal exists only in the person’s mistaken picture of it. For example, someone may imagine that giving in to a shameful desire is a sign of greatness. The person thinks their whole self seeks it, but in fact the imagination and bodily appetite seek a passing pleasure.

You may object: This answer clearly belongs with the preceding question, not with the present one. I reply: it belongs here too. The present objection was that if a goal makes someone act, and the agent is higher than the result it produces, the agent would have to gain some perfection from a goal beneath it. But the soul, considered in its higher nature, does not perform a particular act to gain a passing, lesser goal; such a goal cannot complete it in that respect. When the soul acts through its connection with matter, however, it can act for a particular goal, because in that respect it can gain what it lacks. If the answer also fits the earlier question, that is no difficulty: the earlier question then has two answers.

The commentator says that the world’s true existence depends on God; created things have existence only through Him. In the Persian verse, the word for “or” separates two ideas. It does not show doubt. The heedless may think that some things are enemies and others friends, but all things display the qualities of the true Beloved.
God’s knowledge of Himself is active: it brings things into being.
An action has a goal in the sense that it reaches a fitting result, the fuller state toward which it tends. God’s own goal, in this sense, is Himself.
Harm and loss are called side results because they arise indirectly within the order of material things. God does not directly aim at them.

Nature has a kind of prior awareness because a source must in some way hold the basis for what it produces. The power of fire to heat contains the basis of heat; the power of water to cool contains the basis of cold. The result does not come from a source wholly unrelated to it.
The commentator reads the Qur'anic verb as “they understand,” so the verse says that people do not understand the praise of other things.

The commentator argues that awareness and love appear in every kind of existence, each according to its level. If bodily matter and a higher intellect share the same basic kind of existence, though at very different levels, then even a very faint form of existence has some degree of awareness and love. This is how the author earlier described matter’s natural longing for form.

The saying “God is Zayd’s existence” means that God alone has existence in the fullest and independent sense. Created things do not have existence by themselves; God gives them being and holds them in being. There is no second, separate source of existence. The distinction between a thing and its existence points to this dependence; it is not a separate object added in the mind.

The claim that orderly action proves planning is not a proof. It may persuade people who do not see how natural results follow from the powers of things. Nature can bring about an ordered result without thinking or choosing it.
The two senses are the goal that gives rise to an action and the end at which the action arrives.

The commentator explains three connected senses of the world’s final goal: God’s knowledge of the good order before creation; God Himself as the true end of creation; and God as known and met by those who seek Him. The second is the end reached by creation itself; the third is the end as experienced by creatures who come to know God. These differences matter while the seeker and the One sought are viewed as separate. They disappear in complete awareness of God.
This refers to both kinds of command: the commands of religious law and the commands built into the way creation works.

The commentator says that people attached to worldly things will not be comforted in the next life by imagining those things. When someone loses money or a child, simply imagining them does not ease the grief; it may deepen it. In the next life, people face the real results of their actions: wrongful gain becomes a form of fire, while generosity becomes a good and welcome reality. The next life is the harvest of what people do here.

This conclusion is the finest point in this stage, indeed in all these stages. Understanding it joins the book’s ending to its opening and brings the work to completion. It brings together proof and direct spiritual experience—the kind taught by the All-Merciful when joined with awareness of God—as well as reason and transmitted teaching. May God reward the efforts of the one who brought it to completion.

An intermediary in existence is one that makes a subject truly have the property it mediates; that property cannot truthfully be denied of the subject. Fire, for example, makes water hot. An intermediary in attribution works differently: the subject is described by association, so the description can truthfully be denied of it. There are several kinds. In the first, the intermediary and the subject exist separately and occupy different places, as with a ship and the passenger it carries when both are called moving. In the second, they exist separately but are not apart in place, as blackness and ebony when we call the ebony black; blackness is what is truly black. In the third, they exist as one, as broader kind and distinguishing feature in a definition, and as essence and existence when we consider what is real. Because an individual plays this third kind of role in the realization of a natural universal, the universal exists only through individuals, not separately from them, as the thinker from Hamadan who lived in Avicenna’s time held. Nor does it exist in a separate world as the archetype of its kind, as some have imagined. Such a creative archetype would itself be an individual of that kind; its greater perfection would not prevent it from sharing its nature with other individuals, just as a perfect human being is still human like an imperfect one. In short, the universal does not act as something that gives existence. It has no existence apart from individuals, and its nature is neither existent nor nonexistent in itself. Existence is neither identical with nor part of it. The universal nature is immersed in the existence of its individual; its real existence is that individual’s own existence. So it is not an intermediary in existence but is attributed to the individual by association. This attribution is metaphorical in ordinary thought, though it counts as demonstrative when seen from a high level of spiritual insight.

Scholars disagree about how the parts of a definition, such as a general kind and its distinguishing feature, are joined, although they agree that the mind distinguishes them. One view says that these parts are separate in both essence and existence in the external world. A second says that they are distinct in essence but united in existence, since they are parts that can be predicated of the whole; predication means that they share one existence, while essence is prior to existence in what a thing is. A third view says that they are united in both essence and existence. The author takes a fourth view: these parts have no external reality as separate or unified essences, even though the natural universal exists externally in an incidental way. What exists in itself outside the mind is one simple mode of existence. Depending on its capacities and on which similarities it notices, the mind draws distinct ideas from it. When the author says here and in his other books that the true distinguishing feature is a particular existence, he is expressing this fourth view.

“Relation” here means the way God’s existence shines through the world, not a separate relation between two independent things. The commentator distinguishes the world as God’s shadow from the essences where that shadow appears: existence is light, while essences have no independent being. Saying that the world exists through God does not mean God created a second, separate reality. This is why the Qur'anic verse says, “Have you not seen your Lord?” rather than, “Have you not seen your Lord’s shadow?”

Every image that appears where the shadow falls is a sign of the original reality from which it spreads. The greater world is like a mirror of God’s high attributes and beautiful names, which are the roots of all things. To know the realities of things is, in the end, to know God and His attributes. This also explains “He taught Adam all the names”: the complete human being knows the realities of the world through God, and this knowledge is itself knowledge of God. Readings of the verse in terms of the realities of the world, God’s attributes, or the names of Muhammad and his family support one another.

The commentator says that the verse does not mean God could have held back the shadow but chose not to. God willed the world and brought it about through His generosity and wisdom; all that happens was already known and decreed. The verse uses a conditional form like “If He wills, He can replace you.”
“Universal concepts” here explains “natural universals”: an essence considered just as it is, before the mind considers it as universal.

The commentator explains the familiar saying that possible essences and fixed entities are not beings in themselves but still have effects. They have no existence of their own; they receive a dependent status when existence gives them its features. This lets us speak of possibility, limitation, and multiplicity without treating these ideas as separate beings. Possibility means that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary for an essence; limitation belongs to essence, not existence; and existence does not multiply by itself, but through the things in which it appears.

The comparison shows how concepts such as life, knowledge, and power are drawn from the existence they describe. They are like possible essences drawn from individual beings. The same concept can describe God or an angel, while the relation tells us whether that life or knowledge is eternal or began in time.

Every individual fully has the nature of its kind. The universal’s relation to its individuals is like a parent’s relation to children: the whole nature is present in each individual, with that individual’s features making it particular. The nature is not split into parts or multiplied with the individuals; the difference lies in how the mind considers each one.

The commentator explains the unity of existence: existence has one shared meaning, and what distinguishes each being is not something added from outside. The same existence appears in different particular forms.

The commentator praises the mystery of how God links universal essences with individual existences without a shared part between them. The universal is the particular understood in a different way; the difference lies in how we perceive it. God’s names bring opposites together—the First and the Last, the Visible and the Hidden. The same existence is present in the highest intellects, though it remains free of possibility and change. This is another example of God joining opposites without a common feature between them.

In Sufi language, the “secret of destiny” is God’s eternal knowledge of each fixed essence and of the states it will display when it exists. God judges each thing according to what He knows of it. Some say that knowing this secret frees a person from striving and toil. The commentator notes that this is different from the question of why some evils arise in the world.

The commentator cites Qur'anic verses saying that good comes from God, while evil comes from oneself; that all things come from God; that people will only will what God wills; and that God erases and confirms what He wills. Here, “from yourself” means “from your own fixed essence.”
“Union” here includes all kinds: predication, likeness, sharing a kind, equality, and other forms of sameness, including cases where we do not usually describe them through predication.

An effect is not a separate thing alongside its source; it is the source appearing in another way. The commentator says that all created beings depend entirely on God. Their beings, qualities, and actions are links to the One who sustains them; their appearance is held within His appearance.

The commentator compares this with the idea that God brings things into being by appearing through them: He reveals them and is hidden in their appearance. At the resurrection, His unity removes their separate forms. This does not mean that God changes His nature or that He has children. It means that created things only seemed to be separate from Him; their reality is His ongoing act, as the Qur'an says, “Each day He is at work.”

The objection can be stated in two ways. If the Necessary Being falls under the broad category of relation, it would need a distinguishing feature and would be composite. If it were identical with that broad category, it would be caused by it. The highest category itself is simple, so only the first version leads to composition.

You may say that this strengthens the objection: if the Necessary Being is a cause through His very essence, and a cause precisely as cause ... What was intended is that the apparent separation assumed at first is not real. We may affirm causation, but understand it as the unfolding of His acts, not as an independent union of the kind the Muʿtazilite proposes. For God “neither begets nor is begotten”; rather, “Each day He is engaged in a matter.” — س ره

If a proof is a judgment of the mind, why does the author say that the mind is not the judge? The commentator answers that he means reason by itself, without God’s light. A proof has authority because it is a light from God. The mind recognizes the truth through a light given to it, just as the saying goes: “Know God through God.”

The point is that every category of relation is a kind of essence, but not every identity that depends on a relation belongs to that category. The argument confuses a relation in a thing’s existence with the mind’s separate idea of relation.

The commentator objects that the category of relation is still an essence and cannot be drawn from existence alone. A relation in existence, however, is not a quality that rests on a subject; it is the link by which one thing’s existence depends on another. The mind forms the separate idea of relation by considering the two things and the link between them.
Relation is a concept formed by thought. It follows the way things exist, but the relation itself is not a separate thing in the external world.

The commentator gives two further answers to the problem of time. First, before and after in time are links in existence itself, not the formal category of relation; not every kind of priority or delay belongs to that category. Second, as the Sheikh explains elsewhere, the mind creates the idea of relation. It can consider the earlier and later parts of time together, even though they do not exist together outside the mind.

The author offers another answer: time is one continuous reality, not a set of separate pieces. Its parts are joined in one flowing existence. In that way, the earlier and later moments are together in the continuous whole, while each keeps its own place in the sequence.
The point is that these things have relational existence, not independent existence, as explained earlier.
The alternative would create a circle: possible beings depend on God’s life, knowledge, power, and other perfections. The argument also applies to a possible perfection claimed to belong to God.

This note compares the argument with a later proof in the section on divine things. A possible being cannot depend on something impossible in itself. This also answers al-Dawani’s objection to the principle that the noblest possible being must exist: its supposed cause cannot be a perfection in God that is itself impossible.

The note cites mystics who say that all things are one reality in different forms. The world’s “attributes” are not qualities added to God; they are features of existence considered in relation to its manifestations.

The note lists images that can help explain this relation: a moving flame tracing a circle, motion giving rise to the idea of a path, a flowing present giving rise to time, a mirror and its reflections, and the sea and its waves. It also invokes the Qur'anic image of a lamp within a niche and the sign of unity found in every thing.

Ordinary compounds, such as a body made of matter and form, have distinct parts. Numbers, by contrast, consist of repeated ones. The note also compares this kind of predication to statements about possibility or “thingness,” where the predicate is not an added quality in the subject.
“Existence without restriction” means existence itself, not a general concept. Its all-pervading reach is an act of the Real, not the Real’s essence considered in itself.
The distinction allows two approaches to be reconciled: denying limitations and possible boundaries does not mean denying existence as a positive reality.
Eternal necessity means that a thing exists through itself, apart from every distinct external condition or cause.
Number offers a comparison: its kinds are simple in meaning, and any distinction between broader kind and defining feature in them is a distinction the mind makes.
Fractions belong to the category of relation, not quality, because they are not settled qualities inhering in a subject.

This follows one account given by the mystics. Abd al-Razzaq al-Kashani explains the 'Cloud' mentioned in a report about God as the level of absolute oneness, because no one knows that level but God. It is veiled by divine majesty.

Others take the Cloud to mean the level of unity in which the divine names and attributes appear. A thin cloud hangs between heaven and earth; likewise this level stands between the heaven of undivided oneness and the world of created multiplicity. Kashani rejects this reading of the report. The Prophet was asked where the Lord was before creating the world and answered, 'In a Cloud.' But the level where names and relationships are first distinguished already involves a determination, and Kashani takes everything determined to be created.

I do not accept that every determination must be created. This is the appearance of God's attributes, not yet His acts in the created world. The fixed realities related to the names and attributes appear as objects of divine knowledge. They are not thereby created things existing independently of that knowledge. Even the first active giving of existence is called the world of command rather than the world of creation in this terminology. On the author's account, the separate intellects belong to the divine realm and endure through God's own enduring reality.
Moreover, the question concerned the Lord and the level of lordship. That is precisely the level of unity in which the names and attributes are distinguished, as the author states elsewhere.

The source seems to omit a second “either.” The note supplies it: existence taken with one attribute is a particular name; with all attributes it is the name “Allah”; with a particular created determination it is a particular possible being; and with all such determinations it is the “Great Human,” the universe as a whole.

The note quotes Jami on the fixed entities: before the sea of generosity stirred, they were distinct neither in knowledge nor in external existence; when it stirred, the Necessary and the possible became distinct and the pattern of duality began.

By this he means the universal intellect, which embraces the intellects arranged both in higher and lower ranks and alongside one another. It is the enduring reality at the heart of the world. When philosophers say that ‘substance remains,’ substance can mean what everything else depends upon. In this sense the enduring heart of the world is God's abiding face, even as created natures pass and change. It is also the existence that spreads through all things. This reality is later called the ‘Breath of the All-Merciful.’ That name usually refers to the existence that extends through the whole world. It is applied here to the intellect that contains all other intellects because this intellect receives that existence in its fullness.

It is its first dwelling place, before it divides into many distinct levels—the mother of all places and of the pens. It still remains in the heaven of its own unity. At this level there is no need to treat its essence as something separate from its existence; on the view being defended, intellect has no essence apart from the fact that it exists.

God’s self-sustaining power appears at every level: in the concept of substance in the mind, in matter as the subject of material forms, and in the universal intellect as the form of forms and source of all agents.
Compound divine names, such as the Living, the Self-Sustaining or the Most High, the Magnificent, can have a unity that produces an effect not found in either name taken by itself.

An objection: any two names can be put together. What makes this combination a real unity? The answer is that a being must genuinely display both names, either by its created nature or through the qualities it develops. In its created nature, an animal is both hearing and seeing; the heavens display enduring motion and elevation. In conduct, a person may acquire both wisdom and generosity.

If someone is generous but lacks wisdom, merely calling that person 'the servant of the Generous and Wise' does not bring the two qualities together. In this way, a person who is strongly shaped by one of the divine names may be called its servant even without bearing that name outwardly. The servant of the Guide leads others; the servant of the Giver gives to them.

As explained earlier, things may appear to a seeker as signs in which the divine names are displayed. From a higher point of view, they may be described as the names expressed in action, because the sign has no independent standing apart from what it displays. At the highest level of sincerity, even the distinction of attributes falls away.

The primary names include Living, Knowing, Willing, Powerful, Speaking, Hearing, and Seeing, with “Allah” as their chief. The main names are finite, while their many derivatives are not. “Relation” here includes both pure relations and things described through relations.

Once “name” is understood in the mystics’ sense, sayings such as “the world is a manifestation of the names” or “the name is the named” need not be taken as ordinary identity claims. They are the same in existence but distinct in meaning.
God's essential names belong to the unseen, and His essence—the hidden treasure—is the unseen beyond every unseen thing. This is one reading of the words, “With Him are the keys of the unseen.”

Some writers find a symbolic meaning in the letters of the divine name. The letter ha can stand for pure divine identity rather than for an ordinary pronoun. It may be drawn as a circle, with no starting or ending point and with its center equally related to every part of its edge. Some draw two circles instead, to suggest beauty and majesty. The letter waw arises when the sound is extended. Since ha is formed in the throat and waw at the lips, their joining can suggest the divine breath embracing what is hidden and what is outward. The sound is only a sign pointing toward the unlimited divine existence; it does not contain it.

Alternatively, the 'keys of the unseen' may refer to God's names expressed in action: the intellects through which beings come forth and those through which they return. On either reading, only God knows them fully. Knowledge requires a likeness between the knower and the known. Whatever belongs wholly to the divine realm exists and remains through Him; only He knows its innermost reality.
